n: The priests and the whole tribe of Levi received no tribal land. Instead, they lived on portions of the offerings brought to the Lord.

f.w: the offerings of the LORD made by fire

n: Their inheritance was the Lord himself — a privilege of service rather than property.
When someone offered an ox or sheep for a fellowship meal, the priest received specific cuts as his share.

f.g: What rightfully belonged to the priest.

n: The first of the harvest and the first wool shearing also went to the priest. Giving God the first, not the leftovers, shows trust.

f.g: The wool sheared from a sheep.

n: God chose Levi’s tribe to stand and minister in his name for all generations.
A Levite living in any town could choose to come to the central sanctuary and serve there wholeheartedly.

f.g: Where he was living as a resident (Levites lived scattered among the tribes).

n: Such a Levite had full right to serve alongside the Levites already at the sanctuary.

f.w: as all his brethren the Levites do

n: He shared equally in the food, regardless of any income from selling family property.

f.g: Family inheritance or property passed down from ancestors.

n: Moses now warns against the occult practices of Canaan. Israel must not learn them.
A list of forbidden practices: child sacrifice and various ways of trying to read the future or control spiritual powers.

f.g: Child sacrifice, often linked with the god Molech.
Trying to learn hidden things through omens or lots.
A fortune-teller or one who reads signs to find lucky days.

n: Also forbidden: casting spells and trying to contact the dead. Seeking revelation outside God’s channels is spiritually dangerous.

f.g: A medium who claims to talk with spirits.
One who seeks to consult the dead.

n: These practices were part of why God was removing the Canaanites from the land.
“Perfect” here means wholehearted, complete, or sincere — loyal to God without mixing in other powers.
Other nations turned to fortune-tellers; Israel had something better — the Lord himself speaking through prophets.

f.w: hath not suffered thee so to do

n: A key prophecy: God would raise up a prophet like Moses. Peter, Stephen, and the risen Christ himself identified this Prophet as Jesus.

f.w: a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me
f.r: Acts 3:22-23; Acts 7:37; 1 Nephi 22:20-21; 3 Nephi 20:23; Joseph Smith—History 1:40

n: At Sinai the terrified people had asked Moses to be their go-between, not wanting to hear God’s voice directly again.

f.w: Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD

n: God approved their request; it was wise to have a prophet speak for him.
God’s promise repeated in his own words: he will put his words in the Prophet’s mouth. Jesus said he spoke only what the Father gave him.

f.w: will put my words in his mouth

n: Those who reject the Prophet’s words must answer to God. Peter quoted this as “shall be destroyed from among the people.”

f.w: I will require it of him

n: A false prophet — one who invents messages in God’s name or speaks for other gods — faced death under this law.

f.w: shall presume to speak a word in my name

n: The natural question: how can people tell a true prophet from a false one?
One test: if a prophecy given in the Lord’s name fails, it did not come from him. There is no need to fear such a speaker.

f.w: if the thing follow not, nor come to pass
thou shalt not be afraid of him
f.g: Do not be intimidated by his claims.
